Compatible jets on closed sets

Written by GPT-6.1 Sol (OpenAI), Ultra reasoning effort, September 2026. Checked once by GPT-6.1 Sol (OpenAI), Ultra reasoning effort. Public domain (CC0).

Source/proof self-check and prerequisite integration by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), Ultra, October 2026. Historical authorship and component terms are retained.

Prescribing a function and its derivatives on a closed set is more than assigning numbers at its points. Nearby assignments must fit one Taylor expansion to the required order. Whitney's extension theorem says that this compatibility is exactly what is needed. The proof glues local Taylor polynomials at a scale comparable to the distance from the set. Its estimate then describes what a finite-order distribution supported on that set can measure.

The preceding jet lesson proves smooth mollification, indicator cutoffs, pairings with compactly supported distributions on all suitable smooth functions, and the vanishing-jet theorem. The complete integral Taylor proof supplies every Taylor remainder used here. The kernel lesson supplies support localization and smooth test-space topology. The supplied scalar foundation, §§12–13, proves Euclidean compactness, finite-coordinate calculus, cutoffs and uniform limits; the measure foundation, §§15.0–15.1, provides cube volumes, integration and changes of variables. We prove the full finite-order extension construction, its partition and norm bound below. The references give exact source comparisons and broader jet context.

Every function on a neighborhood of gives a compatible jet. Indeed Taylor's formula for each gives its remainder as , uniformly for nearby points of . We will prove the converse with a bounded linear extension. The word linear refers to the entire family of assigned jet values.

Exercises

Exercise 1 (basic: the order-zero condition). Show that consists of all continuous functions on . Prove that its norm is equivalent to the supremum norm, and explain how Theorem 3.1 supplies a bounded linear compactly supported continuous extension.

Exercise 2 (intermediate: reproducing a polynomial). On the interval , prescribe , , . Verify compatibility for , compute the normalized remainders, and determine the extension before the final cutoff in (3.5). What remains true after that cutoff?

Exercise 3 (intermediate: incompatible assignments). On , prescribe and . Show that both assigned functions are continuous on , but that the jet is not compatible for . Prove directly that no extension could have those traces.

Exercise 4 (advanced: finite and infinite closed supports). Prove that, on a fixed finite set , the norm (1.4) is bounded by a constant times the first jet-value sum alone. Deduce the corresponding bound for every order-at-most- distribution supported in . Compare this with (4.2) and identify the geometric quantity that ceases to be bounded uniformly.

Exercise 5 (advanced: completeness and a projection). Prove that is complete for (1.4). Let denote the functions with bounded continuous derivatives through order , with their global derivative supremum norm. Show that jet restriction is bounded, and that is a bounded projection on , whose kernel consists exactly of functions with all these jets zero on .

Solutions

Solution 1. There is only , and , with diagonal value zero. A continuous function on compact is uniformly continuous, so the compatibility condition holds. Conversely membership already requires continuity of the component. The remainder supremum is at most , so

The theorem with gives a continuous compactly supported extension, linear in the assigned values, with supremum controlled by this norm. This is a statement about continuous extension; differentiability is not asserted at order zero.

Solution 2. At every , the polynomial equals . Thus every difference of Taylor polynomials is zero and all normalized remainders vanish. The jet is compatible. The partition sum off gives , and it has that same value on . After the final cutoff the extension is ; it still equals the polynomial throughout the neighborhood where , including all its prescribed jets on , but it is now compactly supported.

Solution 3. Both components are continuous on this set, including at zero. However , so

It does not tend to the diagonal value zero. If a extension existed, it would satisfy , and . Its difference quotients at zero along this sequence would equal one, contradicting . Continuity of separately assigned derivatives is therefore weaker than Taylor compatibility.

Solution 4. For a singleton, the remainder sum is zero. Otherwise let and . Every numerator in (1.2) is bounded by a fixed finite sum of jet suprema times powers of ; every denominator is at least the corresponding power of . There are finitely many multi-indices, so . The compatibility condition is automatic because off-diagonal pairs do not approach the diagonal. Corollary 4.1 gives the claimed distribution bound. In the infinite example there is no positive minimum separation: . Its tests have uniformly bounded jet values on , yet the remainders divided by that separation grow. Finite-set constants cannot be carried over uniformly to those pairs.

Solution 5. Let be Cauchy in (1.4). Each component converges uniformly on to a continuous . Each remainder converges uniformly on to a continuous function , zero on the diagonal. For , pass to the limit in the finite expression (1.2). It gives for the limiting jet. Thus that jet is compatible, and all its component and remainder differences tend to zero in supremum norm. This is completeness.

Taylor's formula on the whole line segment from to bounds (1.2), for a restricted , by a constant times the global suprema of its derivatives through order . For top derivatives the bound is twice their supremum. Compatibility follows from uniform continuity on a compact neighborhood of , as in the necessity argument. Hence . Theorem 3.1 makes bounded into , and is the identity on . Consequently

If , then . If , apply and use to obtain . This identifies the kernel and proves the projection assertion. Completeness and the projection are consequences of the full remainder norm; they do not justify replacing that norm by pointwise jet values on an arbitrary closed set.
